newsitem.title: USA: SEC chair urges progress on derivatives accounting.
newsitem.headline: SEC chair urges progress on derivatives accounting.

text.p: Arthur Levitt, chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, urged the Financial Accounting Standards Board to move forward with its controversial derivatives accounting project.

"The question of timing is terribly important on any of these contentious issues," Levitt told members of the accounting board at an open meeting of the commission here Monday. "The longer they are allowed to fester, the more difficult it will be to come to closure."
The accounting board released a draft proposal in June to overhaul accounting for derivatives.
Under the proposal, all derivatives would be carried on a company's balance sheet, unlike the present treatment where some derivatives are listed off-balance-sheet.
The proposal would also limit the use of hedge accounting, forcing companies to sometimes report fluctuations in the value of derivatives holdings in net income.

But at public hearings on the draft last month, corporations that use derivatives strongly criticized several aspects of the new accounting rules. They said limits on hedge accounting would create excessive volatility in their earnings.
Despite the criticism, the board plans to begin revising the draft rules soon and aims to complete its work by June 30, 1997, board chairman Dennis Beresford said after the meeting.

"We're still on target for June 30 being our planned date," Beresford said. The board will begin "redeliberations" this month or in January, he said. With all the knotty issues to be addressed, "we probably won't know until about April 1 how likely it is that we'll make the June date."
SEC commissioner Steven Wallman praised the board's work so far but also admonished the board not to disrupt legitimate use of derivatives by companies to manage risk.
"I think it's absolutely critical that sophisticated risk management techniques not be deterred because of the accounting," Wallman said during the meeting.
